claims.text: In our uncalibrated relative phone-audio recordings in the passenger saloon, mean section levels were -18.66 dBFS(A) (n=6, sd=0.35) on eastbound Liverpool Street to Bethnal Green, -19.42 dBFS(A) (n=6, sd=0.35) on eastbound Bethnal Green to Mile End, -18.8 dBFS(A) (n=5, sd=0.48) on westbound Bethnal Green to Liverpool Street, and -19.07 dBFS(A) (n=5, sd=0.65) on westbound Mile End to Bethnal Green.

Across 11 paired trips in our uncalibrated relative phone-audio recordings, Liverpool Street to Bethnal Green was higher than Bethnal Green to Mile End in 10 of 11 trips with a mean within-trip difference of 0.54 dB (range -0.13 to 1.21 dB, sd=0.36, one-sided sign test p=0.0059), so the pre-registered check returned NO-GO because the rule requires Liverpool Street to Bethnal Green to be higher on every trip and one westbound trip went the other way (-0.13 dB); the difference is also below 1 dB, inside the Voice Memos limiter compression and run-to-run variation, and the level variants do not agree in every trip.

In our uncalibrated relative phone-audio measurements, eastbound Liverpool Street to Bethnal Green on the Central line (-18.66 dBFS(A), n=6, sd=0.35) was 6.86 dB higher in relative level than eastbound Aldgate East to Whitechapel on the Hammersmith & City line (-25.52 dBFS(A), n=2, sd=1.89), the quietest section we recorded; because this compares different lines, trains, and tunnel types across rides with uncalibrated audio, it is a weak comparison that shows nothing specific about the Liverpool Street to Bethnal Green track and is not a calibrated dB(A) difference.

Using the NIOSH sound level meter app on an iPhone in the passenger saloon over one whole trip per direction including platform waits and the Bethnal Green dwell, we recorded indicative levels of 91.9 dB(A) LAeq (max 109.7 dB, LCpeak 124.4 dB) eastbound from Liverpool Street to Mile End and 87.3 dB(A) LAeq (max 105.3 dB, LCpeak 120.2 dB) westbound from Mile End to Liverpool Street; because the app on the iPhone built-in microphone is validated only up to about 85 dB(A), below both readings, these readings are indicative and may read low, each direction is a single trip on a different train (so the eastbound-westbound difference may reflect the train rather than the direction or track), and they are not like-for-like with TfL's per-section in-cab figures.

Under The Control of Noise at Work Regulations 2005 (CNAWR) cited by TfL for worker occupational health assessments, the lower exposure action value is a daily personal noise exposure level (LEP,d) of 80 dB(A), the upper exposure action value is 85 dB(A), and the exposure limit value is 87 dB(A).

claims.text: In the documents we reviewed, we found no statement of which track (eastbound, westbound, or both) or which chainages were ground on these sections in the grinding window reported in the Mayor's written answer, no record of grinding on either section since then, no confirmation that the planned Eastbound Liverpool Street to Bethnal Green deep Tube reconditioning was completed, and no TfL in-train noise measurement for either section from before that grinding window (so the reviewed documents cannot show whether grinding lowered noise or whether levels have changed since); because we did not review all of TfL's twice-yearly updates to the Assembly or their attached data packs, TfL may hold or may already have published this information.

In its 20 August 2025 update to the London Assembly, TfL stated that rail corrugation is the main cause of noise and vibration across the network and that it employs a data-led approach that analyses data from the entire network to determine where rail defects occur and establish where corrugation has worsened to tailor and prioritise rail grinding schedules; its 9 August 2024 update reported completing Pandrol Vanguard conversion to Delkor as part of Deep Tube Reconditioning at seven locations with nine sites in process, without naming the sites.

asks.request: Provide all rail grinding completion logs and track chainages (by direction, eastbound and westbound) for the Central line sections between Liverpool Street and Bethnal Green and between Bethnal Green and Mile End from December 2021 to the present, plus any entries on the current eight-week forward rail grinding schedule.
asks.why: Mayor's Question 2022/1791 lists both sections as ground for noise between December 2021 and May 2022 without stating track direction or chainage (C01, C15). TfL states that grinding must be repeated at regular intervals, usually 6 months to a year, to maintain effectiveness, and the Mayor stated that noise grinding is planned once defect grinding is scheduled and spare capacity is identified (C04). The record since May 2022 shows whether these sections have been re-ground.

asks.request: Confirm whether the planned financial year 2023/24 Deep Tube Reconditioning works on the Eastbound Central line between Liverpool Street and Bethnal Green were completed, what track fastenings or works were involved, and the start and completion dates and chainages.
asks.why: TfL's December 2022 letter listed Liverpool Street to Bethnal Green Eastbound for Deep Tube Reconditioning in 2023/24 without specifying what the works at this site involve (C03). TfL's August 2024 update reports conversions completed at seven locations and nine sites in process without naming them, its August 2025 update does not mention this site, and we have not reviewed TfL's other six-monthly updates (C15, C16).

asks.request: Disclose all bi-monthly noise measurements (dB LAeq and LCpeak, eastbound and westbound, specifying whether taken in the cab or passenger saloon) recorded on the Central line for Liverpool Street to Bethnal Green and Bethnal Green to Mile End from January 2021 to the present, and state whether any TfL disclosure or dataset contains the 92.8 dB figure for Liverpool Street to Bethnal Green that Brixton Buzz, crediting JRPass, attributed to 'TfL data'.
asks.why: TfL stated in FOI-1231-2425 that Central line readings are carried out on a bi-monthly period and disclosed 24 June 2024 in-cab figures of 87/86 dB LAeq on LST-BTH and 83/82 dB LAeq on BTH-MLE (C05), while our indicative whole-trip app readings in the passenger saloon were also high (C11) and we have no pre-grinding in-train figures to compare against (C15). A press report attributes a 92.8 dB figure to TfL data, but its source, date, and measurement position are unknown (C14).

asks.request: Provide the most recent rail roughness (corrugation) plots and track inspection reports for both eastbound and westbound tracks on Liverpool Street to Bethnal Green and Bethnal Green to Mile End.
asks.why: TfL previously disclosed January 2018 rail roughness plots for eastbound Bethnal Green to Mile End under FOI-1730-1819 (C02). Its August 2025 update states that its data-led approach analyses data from the entire network to determine where rail defects occur and establish where corrugation has worsened to prioritise rail grinding schedules (C16). Disclosing current roughness data for these two sections would show whether rail roughness is elevated now.

verified_claims.text: In our uncalibrated relative phone-audio recordings in the passenger saloon, mean section levels were -18.66 dBFS(A) (n=6, sd=0.35) on eastbound Liverpool Street to Bethnal Green, -19.42 dBFS(A) (n=6, sd=0.35) on eastbound Bethnal Green to Mile End, -18.8 dBFS(A) (n=5, sd=0.48) on westbound Bethnal Green to Liverpool Street, and -19.07 dBFS(A) (n=5, sd=0.65) on westbound Mile End to Bethnal Green.

Across 11 paired trips in our uncalibrated relative phone-audio recordings, Liverpool Street to Bethnal Green was higher than Bethnal Green to Mile End in 10 of 11 trips with a mean within-trip difference of 0.54 dB (range -0.13 to 1.21 dB, sd=0.36, one-sided sign test p=0.0059), so the pre-registered check returned NO-GO because the rule requires Liverpool Street to Bethnal Green to be higher on every trip and one westbound trip went the other way (-0.13 dB); the difference is also below 1 dB, inside the Voice Memos limiter compression and run-to-run variation, and the level variants do not agree in every trip.

In our uncalibrated relative phone-audio measurements, eastbound Liverpool Street to Bethnal Green on the Central line (-18.66 dBFS(A), n=6, sd=0.35) was 6.86 dB higher in relative level than eastbound Aldgate East to Whitechapel on the Hammersmith & City line (-25.52 dBFS(A), n=2, sd=1.89), the quietest section we recorded; because this compares different lines, trains, and tunnel types across rides with uncalibrated audio, it is a weak comparison that shows nothing specific about the Liverpool Street to Bethnal Green track and is not a calibrated dB(A) difference.

Using the NIOSH sound level meter app on an iPhone in the passenger saloon over one whole trip per direction including platform waits and the Bethnal Green dwell, we recorded indicative levels of 91.9 dB(A) LAeq (max 109.7 dB, LCpeak 124.4 dB) eastbound from Liverpool Street to Mile End and 87.3 dB(A) LAeq (max 105.3 dB, LCpeak 120.2 dB) westbound from Mile End to Liverpool Street; because the app on the iPhone built-in microphone is validated only up to about 85 dB(A), below both readings, these readings are indicative and may read low, each direction is a single trip on a different train (so the eastbound-westbound difference may reflect the train rather than the direction or track), and they are not like-for-like with TfL's per-section in-cab figures.

Under The Control of Noise at Work Regulations 2005 (CNAWR) cited by TfL for worker occupational health assessments, the lower exposure action value is a daily personal noise exposure level (LEP,d) of 80 dB(A), the upper exposure action value is 85 dB(A), and the exposure limit value is 87 dB(A).

verified_claims.text: In the documents we reviewed, we found no statement of which track (eastbound, westbound, or both) or which chainages were ground on these sections in the grinding window reported in the Mayor's written answer, no record of grinding on either section since then, no confirmation that the planned Eastbound Liverpool Street to Bethnal Green deep Tube reconditioning was completed, and no TfL in-train noise measurement for either section from before that grinding window (so the reviewed documents cannot show whether grinding lowered noise or whether levels have changed since); because we did not review all of TfL's twice-yearly updates to the Assembly or their attached data packs, TfL may hold or may already have published this information.

In its 20 August 2025 update to the London Assembly, TfL stated that rail corrugation is the main cause of noise and vibration across the network and that it employs a data-led approach that analyses data from the entire network to determine where rail defects occur and establish where corrugation has worsened to tailor and prioritise rail grinding schedules; its 9 August 2024 update reported completing Pandrol Vanguard conversion to Delkor as part of Deep Tube Reconditioning at seven locations with nine sites in process, without naming the sites.

asks.request: Provide all rail grinding completion logs and track chainages (by direction, eastbound and westbound) for the Central line sections between Liverpool Street and Bethnal Green and between Bethnal Green and Mile End from December 2021 to the present, plus any entries on the current eight-week forward rail grinding schedule.
asks.why: Mayor's Question 2022/1791 lists both sections as ground for noise between December 2021 and May 2022 without stating track direction or chainage (C01, C15). TfL states that grinding must be repeated at regular intervals, usually 6 months to a year, to maintain effectiveness, and the Mayor stated that noise grinding is planned once defect grinding is scheduled and spare capacity is identified (C04). The record since May 2022 shows whether these sections have been re-ground.

asks.request: Confirm whether the planned financial year 2023/24 Deep Tube Reconditioning works on the Eastbound Central line between Liverpool Street and Bethnal Green were completed, what track fastenings or works were involved, and the start and completion dates and chainages.
asks.why: TfL's December 2022 letter listed Liverpool Street to Bethnal Green Eastbound for Deep Tube Reconditioning in 2023/24 without specifying what the works at this site involve (C03). TfL's August 2024 update reports conversions completed at seven locations and nine sites in process without naming them, its August 2025 update does not mention this site, and we have not reviewed TfL's other six-monthly updates (C15, C16).

asks.request: Disclose all bi-monthly noise measurements (dB LAeq and LCpeak, eastbound and westbound, specifying whether taken in the cab or passenger saloon) recorded on the Central line for Liverpool Street to Bethnal Green and Bethnal Green to Mile End from January 2021 to the present, and state whether any TfL disclosure or dataset contains the 92.8 dB figure for Liverpool Street to Bethnal Green that Brixton Buzz, crediting JRPass, attributed to 'TfL data'.
asks.why: TfL stated in FOI-1231-2425 that Central line readings are carried out on a bi-monthly period and disclosed 24 June 2024 in-cab figures of 87/86 dB LAeq on LST-BTH and 83/82 dB LAeq on BTH-MLE (C05), while our indicative whole-trip app readings in the passenger saloon were also high (C11) and we have no pre-grinding in-train figures to compare against (C15). A press report attributes a 92.8 dB figure to TfL data, but its source, date, and measurement position are unknown (C14).

asks.request: Provide the most recent rail roughness (corrugation) plots and track inspection reports for both eastbound and westbound tracks on Liverpool Street to Bethnal Green and Bethnal Green to Mile End.
asks.why: TfL previously disclosed rail roughness plots for eastbound Bethnal Green to Mile End under FOI-1730-1819 (C02). Its August 2025 update states that its data-led approach analyses data from the entire network to determine where rail defects occur and establish where corrugation has worsened to prioritise rail grinding schedules (C16). Disclosing current roughness data for these two sections would show whether rail roughness is elevated now.
